slides.title: Who may even get the bytes?
slides.text: Read decides who can open data. Three more things a rule can allow decide who can carry it: {want}, {keep} and {sync}. Carriers never see the rules themselves: those are sealed for readers. Whoever asks shows their own proof.
list: want: may ask for this data and receive it, sealed.
keep: may store it for good.
sync: may pass it on to others whose rules say want.
slides.deep: want, keep and sync are operations in rules, like any other. Rules are sealed for readers; a carrier only checks the proof chain that the asker presents.

slides.title: want
slides.text: Before a device sends anything, even sealed chunks, the asker shows a proof that a rule gives them want. The carrier checks the signatures and nothing else. A stranger gets nothing at all, not even ciphertext to count or keep. Read includes want.
slides.deep: The asker presents a proof chain: seal → owner → rule granting want to a role → the asker's identity in that role → the asker's registered signer. Valid chain: sealed chunks are sent. No chain: nothing, not even ciphertext.

slides.title: keep
slides.text: Your backup gets want and keep. It holds every sealed chunk, for good, and gives them back to your new phone. It has no read, so to it they're just sealed bytes.
slides.deep: keep means the carrier stores sealed chunks durably and serves them to askers holding want. It never holds a data key.

slides.title: sync
slides.text: The street's always-on peer gets sync. It passes your changes between Alice and Bob when they're never online at the same time. It keeps them only as long as it has to.
slides.deep: sync means the peer may forward sealed chunks to others whose rules give them want, which bridges devices that are never online at the same time.

slides.title: What a carrier sees.
slides.text: Sealed chunks, the hashes that link them, and the proofs it needs to decide whom to give them to. It can store, count and forward them. It can't read a title, a tick, a rule or a frame of the movie.
slides.deep: Visible to a carrier: chunk hashes, sizes, links between chunks, and the proofs needed to decide whom to serve. Invisible: content, rules and keys.

slides.title: All the rules on one list.
slides.text: One piece of data, one owner, three roles, each with exactly what it needs.
slides.deep: One owner, three roles: readers and writers (home), a durable carrier (backup) and a forwarding carrier (street). Each role holds exactly the operations it needs.

slides.title: Alice and Bob, never online together.
slides.text: Alice ticks milk on the train and goes offline. The street's peer picks it up, the backup keeps it, and Bob's laptop gets it in the evening. Neither carrier read a word.
slides.deep: Store-and-forward over carriers: every hop checks want, holds only sealed chunks, and is replaceable. This is the local-first “cloud peer”.

slides.title: Carriers, in short.
list: want, keep and sync decide who may carry data; read decides who may open it.
Carriers check proofs and hold sealed chunks only.
Devices that are never online together still sync, through carriers.
slides.deep: Store-and-forward peers are replaceable and never trusted with content.
